essays.stem: Your team of four must make ten steel window grilles in one week. Describe how you would plan the job and share out the work.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would study the drawing and the order, and list every task: measuring, cutting, marking out, fitting, welding, grinding, inspection, painting and delivery. I would estimate how long each task takes and put them in order on a simple bar chart, showing which tasks depend on others. I would check that the materials, consumables and equipment are available, and order anything missing early. Then I would share the tasks by skill and qualification: for example, the most skilled welder on welding, a careful member on cutting and marking out, and a newer member on grinding and painting with support. I would plan hold points to check the first grille before making the rest. I would brief the team at a toolbox talk on the plan, safety and quality, and check they understand. Each day I would compare progress with the plan, adjust if needed and keep my supervisor informed.
markingPoints: Lists all tasks from the drawing and order
Estimates times and puts tasks in order on a chart
Checks materials and equipment and orders early
Shares work by skill and qualification, with support for newer members
Hold points, briefing, daily monitoring and reporting

essays.stem: Explain how you would run an effective toolbox talk at the start of a day's work in the welding shop.
essays.modelAnswer: I would hold it at the same time each day, at the work area, and keep it short, about ten to fifteen minutes. I would prepare by looking at the day's tasks and the hazards they bring, such as hot work, lifting, grinding or work at height. I would start with the plan for the day and who is doing what. Then I would talk about one or two main hazards and the controls, for example the fire watch for cutting near the door, or the fume extraction for galvanised steel. I would use plain words, show the equipment where it helps, and ask questions to check people understood. I would invite the team to raise concerns or near misses. I would note any actions and who will do them. At the end everyone signs the attendance sheet, and I keep it with the job records. If someone arrives late, I brief them before they start work.
markingPoints: Short, regular, at the work area
Prepared from the day's tasks and hazards
Covers the plan, the main hazards and controls in plain words
Checks understanding and invites concerns
Records attendance and actions; briefs latecomers

essays.stem: Two members of your team have fallen out and it is affecting the work. Describe how you would deal with it.
essays.modelAnswer: I would act early, before it grows. First I would talk to each person privately and calmly, and listen to their side without taking sides. I would try to find the real cause: it may be about a task, a tool, workload, a misunderstanding or something personal. Then, if both agree, I would bring them together in a quiet place and help them talk it through with respect, keeping to the facts and the work. I would help them agree a solution, for example a fair schedule for shared equipment or clearer roles. I would remind them of the Centre's rules on behaviour. I would write down what was agreed and check later that it is working. If the conflict involves bullying, harassment or a safety risk, or it cannot be settled, I would report it to my supervisor and follow the Centre's procedure. Throughout, I would keep the matter confidential.
markingPoints: Acts early; talks to each privately and listens without taking sides
Finds the real cause
Brings them together to agree a solution
Records the agreement and follows up
Refers serious or unresolved cases to the supervisor; keeps it confidential

essays.stem: Explain how a team leader monitors progress on a job, and what to do when the team falls behind the plan.
essays.modelAnswer: I would set clear targets for each day from the plan, such as the number of parts cut or joints welded. I would check progress at set times, by walking the job, asking the team and counting completed work, and mark it on the progress chart. I would also check quality, because work that must be redone is not progress. If we fall behind, I would first find the cause: missing materials, a broken machine, absence, rework or a task that was under-estimated. Then I would agree a fix with the team, for example moving a person to the slow task, getting the machine repaired, or changing the order of work. If needed, I would ask my supervisor for extra help or approved overtime. I would not cut safety or inspection to catch up. I would tell my supervisor early if the finish date is at risk, and record what happened so that future plans are better.
markingPoints: Sets daily targets from the plan
Checks and records progress and quality at set times
Finds the cause of delay
Agrees a fix; asks for help or overtime if needed, never cutting safety
Tells the supervisor early and records lessons

essays.stem: A team member's welds keep failing inspection. Explain how you would give feedback and coach them to improve.
essays.modelAnswer: I would speak to them privately, soon after the problem, and stay calm and respectful. I would start with what they do well, then show them the actual faults on the welds and the inspection result, keeping to facts about the work, not the person. I would ask them what they think is causing it, because they may know about a problem with the machine or the materials. Then I would demonstrate the correct method myself, or ask a skilled welder to, and have them practise on scrap while I watch. I would give clear, specific tips, such as changing the gun angle or travel speed. We would agree a short plan, for example practice pieces each morning for a week, and a check at the end of it. I would praise improvement. I would record the coaching and the results. If there is no improvement, I would discuss further training with my supervisor.
markingPoints: Private, timely, respectful; facts about the work
Asks for their view of the cause
Demonstrates and watches practice with specific tips
Agrees an improvement plan and follow-up; praises progress
Records it and refers for training if needed

essays.stem: Describe the responsibilities of a team leader for health and safety in a welding and fabrication team.
essays.modelAnswer: The team leader must make sure the work is planned safely. This means identifying the hazards of each task and checking that risk assessments and controls are in place, such as screens, fume extraction, fire extinguishers and guards. The leader checks that each person has the training and PPE they need and uses it correctly, and that equipment is checked before use. Hot work, confined space or lifting permits must be in place where needed. The leader briefs the team at toolbox talks and sets a good example by always following the rules. Team members must feel able to stop unsafe work and report hazards without blame. Any incident, injury or near miss must be reported and recorded, and its cause looked into so it does not happen again. The leader keeps first-aid arrangements and emergency exits known to the team. Finally, the leader reports safety problems they cannot fix to the supervisor.
markingPoints: Identifies hazards and checks risk assessments and controls
Training, PPE and equipment checks; permits where needed
Briefs the team and sets the example
Encourages stopping and reporting unsafe work
Records and investigates incidents; first aid and emergencies; reports upwards

essays.stem: Compare a directive (autocratic) leadership style with a participative (democratic) style, and say when a team leader should use each.
essays.modelAnswer: In a directive style, the leader decides and tells the team what to do, with little discussion. It is quick and clear, so it suits emergencies, such as a fire or an injury, and situations where there is only one safe way to do the job, or where the team is new and inexperienced. Used all the time, it can make people feel ignored and lower their motivation. In a participative style, the leader asks the team for ideas and involves them in decisions, while still taking responsibility. It builds commitment, uses the team's knowledge and often finds better solutions. It suits planning a job, improving a process or solving a quality problem, especially with an experienced team. It is slower, so it does not suit urgent decisions. A good team leader changes style to fit the situation and the people: directive when speed and safety demand it, and participative when there is time and the team's experience can help.
markingPoints: Describes the directive style
When directive suits: emergencies, one safe way, new team; drawbacks
Describes the participative style
When participative suits: planning, improvement, experienced team; slower
Good leaders adapt their style to the situation

essays.stem: Explain how you would induct a new member into your fabrication team.
essays.modelAnswer: I would plan the induction before they arrive and make them feel welcome on the first day. I would introduce them to the team and to key people such as the supervisor, the store clerk and the first aider. I would show them the workshop: emergency exits, assembly point, fire extinguishers, first-aid kit and welfare areas. I would explain the safety rules, PPE, hot work rules and how to report hazards and incidents, and check that they have the right PPE. I would explain the job we are working on, their role and who to ask for help. I would check their skills and qualifications before giving them tasks, and pair them with an experienced member for the first days. I would explain working hours, breaks and the Centre's policies. I would check their understanding and have them sign the induction checklist. After the first week I would meet them again to see how they are settling in and answer questions.
markingPoints: Planned and welcoming; introduces people
Site tour: exits, extinguishers, first aid, welfare
Safety rules, PPE and reporting
Explains the job and role; checks skills; pairs with a buddy
Policies, signed checklist and follow-up

essays.stem: Explain how a team leader can communicate clearly with a team in a noisy workshop, where members have different backgrounds and reading levels.
essays.modelAnswer: For important instructions I would move to a quiet area or turn off nearby machines, so everyone can hear. I would use short sentences and plain words, explain any trade terms and avoid slang that some people may not know. I would show as well as tell: point at the drawing, show the part, or demonstrate the method. I would use pictures, sketches and marked-up drawings for people who find reading hard, and not embarrass anyone about their reading. I would ask people to repeat back key points and invite questions. For changes, I would issue the new drawing or a written note and brief everyone, rather than passing messages through one person. In the noisy area, I would agree simple hand signals for stop, wait and come here. I would respect different backgrounds, ages and beliefs, listen as well as speak, and watch for body language that shows someone is unsure. I would follow up later to check the message was understood.
markingPoints: Quiet place for important instructions; plain words, terms explained
Shows as well as tells; uses pictures and drawings
Checks understanding by repeat-back and questions
Written changes to all; agreed hand signals in noise
Respects differences, listens and follows up

essays.stem: Describe what should go into a team leader's end-of-job report to the supervisor, and why each part is useful.
essays.modelAnswer: The report should start with the job details: the job number, client and dates, so it can be filed and found. It should compare the results with the plan: what was made, the time taken and the materials used, so future jobs can be planned and priced better. It should give the quality results: inspection results, rejects and rework, so quality problems can be tracked. It should list any safety incidents, injuries or near misses and what was done, so that lessons are shared. It should record equipment faults and any shortages, so they can be fixed. It should say how the team performed, giving credit where it is due and noting any training needs. It should list problems met and what the team learned, with suggestions for next time. The report should be clear, accurate and honest, dated and signed, with photos or charts where they help.
markingPoints: Job details for filing
Results against plan: output, time and materials
Quality and safety results
Equipment faults, team performance and training needs
Lessons and suggestions; clear, honest, dated and signed

practical1.title: Plan and lead a small fabrication job as a team, with each member leading one stage
practical1.brief: As a team, make four simple steel shelf brackets (or another small item the assessor gives you) to a drawing, in the time allowed. First, write a team work plan on the sheet provided: the task list, a simple bar chart, who does each task, the materials and tools, the hold points for inspection and the main hazards. Each member then leads one stage of the job: for example, the toolbox talk; marking out and cutting; fit-up and tacking; welding; and inspection and clean-up. The stage leader gives the instructions, checks that others understand, keeps the stage on time and records progress on a board or chart. At each hold point, the stage leader checks the work against the drawing before the next stage starts. At the end, hold a five-minute debrief and write down what went well and what to improve. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the brackets, the plan and the debrief notes are finished and the area is clean.
materials: Drawing of the item from the assessor
Steel flat bar or angle as the drawing states
Work plan sheet, progress board or chart paper and markers
Cutting, marking out and measuring tools; MMAW or MIG welding station
photos: The completed team work plan with the bar chart and task owners
The toolbox talk taking place, with the attendance sheet
Each stage leader briefing the team at their stage
The progress board part way through the job
A hold-point check against the drawing
checklist: Helped write a realistic plan with tasks, times, owners and hold points
Led their stage: gave clear instructions and checked understanding
Kept their stage on time and updated the progress record
Checked work at the hold point and acted on any fault
Followed others' instructions and supported the team
Followed safe working practices and wore the right PPE
Took part in the debrief with a useful point
safety: Wear the PPE for each task: safety glasses, gloves, welding helmet, boots
Weld and cut behind screens; keep an extinguisher at hand
Check guards and discs on grinders before use
Treat cut and welded parts as hot
Keep walkways clear of offcuts and leads
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Team meeting role play: solve a workplace problem, agree actions and write a progress report
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your team a job situation card: for example, a delivery of steel is late, two welders disagree over the use of a machine, and the first welds have failed inspection, all on a job due on Friday. Take turns to act as team leader for three short meetings (about 10–15 minutes each): a daily progress meeting, a meeting to sort out the disagreement, and a meeting to find the cause of the failed welds. The other members play team members, using the role cards the assessor gives. In each meeting the leader keeps to an agenda, lets everyone speak, uses a problem-solving method (such as the 5 whys) where it fits, and agrees actions with names and dates. One member takes notes in each meeting. Then, as a team, write a one-page progress report to the supervisor: progress against the plan, the problems, the actions agreed and any help needed. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the notes and the report are finished.
materials: Job situation card and role cards from the assessor
Agenda sheets, action list sheets and a progress report form
Flip chart or whiteboard and markers
A copy of the job plan (bar chart) given with the situation card
photos: The first meeting in progress, with the leader at the board
The problem-solving notes (for example the 5 whys) on the board
The second and third meetings in progress
The completed action lists with names and dates
checklist: As leader, kept to the agenda and let everyone speak
As leader, stayed calm and fair when handling the disagreement
Used a clear method to find the cause of a problem
Agreed actions with names and dates
As a member, listened, gave useful ideas and respected others
Took clear notes when it was their turn
Helped write an accurate, clear progress report
safety: Keep the meeting area clear of trip hazards such as bags and cables
Keep role play respectful: no real personal remarks
If the room is in the workshop, wear the PPE the area needs and stay out of work zones
